newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Privatisation begets Malaysia conglomerate.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Privatisation begets Malaysia conglomerate.

text.p: A management buyout of a Malaysian government property firm has spawned overnight a huge conglomerate -- making millionaires of the managers -- in the latest chapter of Malaysia's ambitious privatisation programme.

On August 22, 14 senior managers of Perbadanan Nasional (Pernas) took control of the privatised company, which in its heyday was used as a vehicle to take over British concerns in the post-colonial era.
The new entity, Pernas International Holdings Bhd (PIHB), has emerged as Malaysia's biggest hotel operator with 11 now in the stable and two more on the drawing board.
PIHB suddenly became a dominant force in the palm oil sector with 195,000 acres (79,000 hectares) under cultivation and plans to expand to 300,000 acres (121,400 hectares) in five years.
It also wound up with a controlling stake in Malayawata Steel and two other listed firms, along with construction and engineering companies.

"For a little less than 500 million ringgit ($200 million), the 14 individuals have gained control of a robust and healthy conglomerate with net assets of more than three billion ringgit...," the Business Times daily said in a commentary.

The privatisation was a two-step process. Pernas' assets were injected into PIHB for 1.15 billion ringgit. The managers then took a controlling 32 percent stake in the enlarged PIHB for 495 million ringgit.
The money will be loaned to them by a local bank "on very favourable terms", Shahriman Tunku Sulaiman, Pernas chairman for the past 20 years, told analysts and journalists.
BIGGEST MANAGEMENT BUYOUT IN MALAYSIAN HISTORY
The deal was striking, not only because it was the biggest management buyout in Malaysian history, but also because there was so little fuss over the demise of Pernas.
Pernas was set up in 1969, after racial riots between Malays and Chinese, to build wealth among "Bumiputras" (native sons) in an economy long dominated by ethnic Chinese.
Pernas was in charge of seizing control of the country's major economic assets, such as then plantation-based Sime Darby Bhd, which was itself privatised years later.
Its importance waned when Permodalan Nasional Bhd became the force for creating Bumiputra wealth through unit trusts. Sime and other firms were sold to PNB at bargain prices.
The end of Pernas reflects a major shift in government thinking, starting from about five years ago, analysts say.
SHIFT IN GOVERNMENT POLICY
The Malay-dominated government is no longer so concerned with creating a large pool of Bumiputra entrepreneurs.
Privatisation contracts have usually gone to a small group of politically well-connected Malays who, the government believes, have the wherewithal to handle big projects.

Last year's privatisation of Hicom Holdings Bhd, a conglomerate which manufactures the Malaysian-made Proton car, and the sale of Malaysian Airline System Bhd the year before, followed a familiar pattern.
Hicom was sold to Yahaya Ahmad, who heads the automotive firm Diversified Resources Bhd.

Tajudin Ramli took a controlling 32 percent stake in Malaysian Airlines for 1.79 billion ringgit in the largest privatisation deal to date, after negotiating the biggest personal loan ever granted in Malaysia.
Tajudin is among a group of bumiputra tycoons known as "Daim's boys", executives who used to work in companies owned by former finance minister Daim Zainuddin.
Daim, himself a self-made billionaire and author of the government's privatisation programme, is believed to have helped Yahaya secure a 1.7 billion ringgit offshore loan to finance the Hicom deal.
Jomo Sundaram, an economics professor at the University of Malaya who has written extensively about Malaysia's privatisation programme, said the Pernas case broke a pattern.
"At least in this case, it was a management buyout. The company was turned over to a group that one presumes has a demonstrated competency and track record.
"That has not always been the case in the past," he added.
Jomo was critical of the privatisation programme for selling off state assets at bargain-basement prices.
OBJECTIVES OF PRIVATISATION

The objectives of privatisation in cutting government spending, generating revenue and deepening the capital markets, have been subordinated to the "Malay wealth-enhancing objective, particularly to the politically well-connected".

Malaysia's privatisation policy drew criticism at last year's party convention of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) for benefiting the few. Some analysts say it may come up again at this year's convention in October.

Mahathir told the convention last year the government wanted "talented, responsible and serious entrepreneurs" for projects. It was better than the old way of handing out shares, land or licences to bumiputras "without taking into account their performance, background or capabilities".
Hicom and MAS were sold to Tajudin and Yahaya because they could raise the money and the government believed those who owned stakes in companies managed them better, Mahathir said.
But critics say Mahathir's privatisation policy smacks of cronyism and poses certain risks for foreign investors.

"The problem is, such local businessmen tend to ride on the coat tails of prominent political figures whose rise and fall add to uncertainty about the business environment," said a report by Political & Economic Risk Consultancy on Malaysia.
"Foreign investors looking for long-term business partners, therefore, face the possibility of exposing themselves to substantial political risk."

It is an open secret, for instance, that there is no love lost between deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim -- Mahathir's heir apparent -- and Daim, his predecessor at the finance ministry and UMNO's current treasurer.
Another of "Daim's boys" stands to gain in the next project up on the privatisation block -- state-run railway KTM Bhd.
A three-party consortium led by Renong Bhd, along with Bolton Properties Bhd and Diversified Resources has been, in principle, awarded the railway privatisation.

One the companies is headed by Daim proteges -- Renong executive chairman Halim Saad. Like Tajudin and other bumiputra tycoons, Halim worked for Daim in the state property firm Peremba Bhd in the 1980s.
Malaysia's 1996-2000 Five-Year Plan, unveiled in May, identified 23 other major projects slated for privatisation.
OTHER PROJECTS SALTED FOR PRIVATISATION
They include debt-laden Perwaja Steel, which was recently awarded to small Bumiputra-owned steel firm Maju Holdings.
Other privatisation projects include the nation's second largest bank, Bank Bumiputra Malaysia; Bank Simpanan Nasional, several highways, ports, hospitals and government agencies.

Privatisation has played a key role in bringing in new technology and attracting foreign funds since most of the projects involved a foreign tie-up, a stock exchange listing or, as in the case of Pernas, a new share issue, analysts said.

"One of the aims of privatisation in Malaysia has been to deepen the capital markets and to use the capital markets to raise money for infrastructure projects," said Chan Kok Peng, Credit Lyonnais' economist in Singapore.
"Certainly as far as attracting foreign capital to Malaysia, privatisation has been a big success," he said.
But a research manager for a local brokerage said Malaysia may be trying to take it too far by privatising things like roads and the Malaysian Tourism Board.
"A line has to be drawn," the manager said. "You can't privatise everything. You have to ask the question: Does it increase costs or lower costs for the consumer?" ($1 = 2.50 ringgit)
